name: Skincare 'skin cycling'
lead: Skin cycling is a rotating skincare routine that alternates nights of chemical exfoliant and retinoid with nights of recovery, so that active ingredients can be used for smoother, clearer, more even-toned skin with less irritation. People follow it to work toward fewer fine lines and dark spots, a brighter complexion and less peeling and redness than daily active use can cause [1].

According to Grokipedia, it was created by New York dermatologist Whitney Bowe, introduced in April 2021, and spread on TikTok in 2022, where the page reports more than 3.5 billion views [1]. The structure is four nights: an AHA or BHA exfoliant, a retinoid, and two recovery nights built around moisturizing and barrier-supporting products, with sunscreen every morning [1].

The same source reports that no published clinical studies have tested skin cycling specifically, and that dermatologists quoted describe it as a practical, adaptable framework [1]. Its building blocks, topical retinoids, are established treatments for acne and photoaging [2].
infobox: AHA/BHA exfoliant, retinol or tretinoin, barrier-supporting moisturizers [1]

paras: The reported four-night cycle is: night one, a gentle chemical exfoliant such as an AHA (glycolic or lactic acid) or BHA (salicylic acid) in place of a physical scrub; night two, retinol or prescription tretinoin on clean, dry skin; nights three and four, recovery with hydrating and barrier-supporting products. Mornings use a gentle cleanser, optional moisturizer and a broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, since exfoliants and retinoids increase sun sensitivity [1].

Recovery-night products described in the source include humectants such as hyaluronic acid and glycerin, ceramides for the lipid barrier, niacinamide, squalane, and pre- and postbiotics [1]. A gentle version adds recovery nights or introduces one active at a time for sensitive skin, eczema or beginners; an advanced version uses fewer recovery nights for people who tolerate retinoids well, usually adjusting after about two weeks without irritation [1].

sections.h: How it is meant to work
paras: The page describes retinoids and acids as speeding cell turnover while also weakening the skin barrier, raising water loss and triggering inflammation, and proposes that recovery periods let the barrier rebuild lipids and proteins [1]. Bowe attributes the purging some users report to overuse rather than a true purge [1]. Topical retinoids are commonly used for acne and photoaging, and only limited amounts are absorbed through the skin [2].

Claimed benefits include better hydration, less sensitivity and a healthier glow within a few cycles, and over time improvement in fine lines and dark spots, along with less redness, peeling and stinging than daily use [1]. The routine is described as suited to sensitive, acne-prone and barrier-compromised skin, and visible change is reported to take eight weeks or more [1].

No studies found. Grokipedia states that no published clinical studies have tested the skin cycling regimen itself [1]. The ingredients it uses have their own literature as treatments for acne and photoaging [2].

Per Grokipedia, dermatologists Melanie Kingsley, Joshua Zeichner, Brendan Camp and Sarah Boyce Sawyer have commented. Kingsley calls it a well-formulated option and Zeichner a reasonable approach for irritation-prone skin, while noting that retinoid data mainly supports daily use for best results; Camp and Boyce Sawyer value its structure and customizability. Overall the page describes it as not revolutionary but a practical, adaptable framework [1]. Results may be slower for people whose skin already tolerates daily actives, and it is not described as a substitute for medical treatment of conditions such as cystic acne or melasma [1].

Overuse of actives can cause irritation, dryness and increased sun sensitivity [1]. Wikipedia states that the American Academy of Dermatology advises against retinoid use in pregnancy, while topical tretinoin is of less concern because limited amounts are absorbed [2].

Bowe markets related products, including a recovery-night cream and a skin cycling program bundle, and the source repeats the brand claim that the cream is clinically proven to repair the barrier [1].

timeline.event: Whitney Bowe introduces the method in April [1]

card.summary: TikTok-famous four-night rotation of exfoliant, retinoid and two recovery nights; reasonable by derm convention but never trialled.
card.note: No clinical studies of the routine itself.

quick.overview:
Skin cycling rotates an exfoliant night, a retinoid night and two recovery nights. It was popularised by dermatologist Whitney Bowe and spread on TikTok.

No clinical studies test the routine; dermatologists quoted describe it as a sensible, adaptable framework.
quick.mechanism: Spacing out actives is meant to limit irritation and give the skin barrier time to recover.
quick.risks: Retinoid and exfoliant irritation is possible; retinoid use in pregnancy is advised against by the AAD.

chain: Exfoliant night and retinoid night alternate with recovery nights
Skin barrier gets time to rebuild between actives
Retinoid and exfoliant tolerated, with smoother, more even, brighter skin over weeks
angle.text: The routine is a way of using retinoids and exfoliating acids, the ingredients associated with smoother texture, fewer fine lines and clearer skin, while limiting the dryness and redness that make people stop using them.
